questions.q: A 30-year-old man from rural Bihar presents with a hypopigmented anaesthetic patch on the forearm, thickened great auricular nerve, and slit-skin smear showing 4+ bacilli. Which leprosy type does this represent?
questions.exp: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) shows high bacterial load (4+ on SSS), multiple lesions with poor sensation, and diffuse nerve thickening. LL is at the anergic pole — abundant bacilli, weak CMI.

questions.q: A patient on multidrug therapy for lepromatous leprosy develops sudden onset of erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL). Which immunological mechanism underlies this reaction?
questions.exp: ENL (Type 2 lepra reaction) is an immune complex–mediated phenomenon (Type III hypersensitivity) with complement activation, neutrophil influx, and deposition of IgG/IgM complexes in tissues.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters involving the oral mucosa and scalp. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular IgG deposition in a 'chicken-wire' pattern. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris shows suprabasal acantholysis, positive Nikolsky sign, mucosal involvement, and DIF with intercellular IgG (and C3) in a 'fish-net/chicken-wire' pattern. Target antigen is desmoglein 3.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman presents with tense blisters on the trunk and limbs without mucosal involvement. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. The target antigen is most likely:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid targets BP180 (BPAG2) and BP230. DIF shows linear IgG/C3 at the BMZ. It is the most common autoimmune blistering disease in the elderly and rarely involves mucosae.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on elbows, knees, and buttocks. DIF shows granular IgA at the dermal papillary tips. Which associated systemic condition must be screened for?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is pathognomonic for glutensensitive enteropathy. Granular IgA at papillary tips on DIF is characteristic. Most patients have subclinical coeliac disease; skin clears on a gluten-free diet plus dapsone.

questions.q: A child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains. Which organism is the most common causative agent of this non-bullous form?
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is predominantly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS), though mixed infection with S. aureus is common. The bullous form is exclusively S. aureus (phage group 2, exfoliative toxin).

questions.q: A diabetic patient develops rapidly spreading painful erythema, warmth, and peau d'orange appearance of the lower leg with systemic toxicity. The most appropriate initial management is:
opts: Oral cetirizine for presumed contact dermatitis
IV antibiotics targeting Group A Streptococcus
questions.exp: This is erysipelas/cellulitis. Peau d'orange, sharp margins, lymphatic involvement, and systemic signs indicate GAS infection. IV penicillin/amoxicillin-clavulanate is first-line; add anti-staphylococcal cover in diabetics.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with a well-demarcated, scaly, hypopigmented patch on the upper back that fluoresces golden-yellow under Wood's lamp. KOH mount shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. Treatment of choice?
opts: Topical selenium sulfide or ketoconazole shampoo
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor caused by Malassezia furfur shows golden-yellow fluorescence under Wood's lamp and hyphae+spores ('spaghetti and meatballs') on KOH. Topical selenium sulfide or azoles are first-line; oral therapy for extensive disease.

questions.q: A gardener presents with a painless papule on the finger that ulcerates and progresses with lymphatic nodules up the forearm. No systemic symptoms. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis caused by Sporothrix schenckii classically presents as sporotrichoid (ascending lymphocutaneous) spread. Associated with thorn/plant injury. Treatment: oral itraconazole (preferred) or potassium iodide.

questions.q: A 5-year-old with tinea capitis shows a fluorescent patch under Wood's lamp (blue-green). Culture shows macroconidia with thick walls and spines. The organism is:
questions.exp: Microsporum canis produces blue-green fluorescence under Wood's lamp (ectothrix infection). It shows thick-walled, spindle-shaped macroconidia with transverse septa and rough walls. T. tonsurans (endothrix, no fluorescence) is most common in India.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HSV-2 positive patient presents with recurrent painful grouped vesicles on the genitals. Which antiviral reduces frequency of recurrence when taken as daily suppressive therapy?
opts: Valacyclovir 1g once daily for 5 days only during outbreaks
questions.exp: Acyclovir 400 mg BD (or valacyclovir 500 mg OD) as daily suppressive therapy reduces recurrence by ~70-80% and decreases viral shedding, thus reducing transmission. Long-term safety is well established.

questions.q: A 3-year-old presents with multiple small flesh-colored umbilicated papules on the trunk and face. The child is immunocompetent. Which statement about this condition is TRUE?
opts: It is caused by herpes simplex virus
It is caused by a poxvirus and is usually self-limiting
Immediate systemic antiviral therapy is required
Wood's lamp examination shows bright white fluorescence
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a poxvirus. In immunocompetent children, it is self-limiting (resolves in 6-18 months). Treatment (cantharidin, curettage) is optional. Large/coalescing lesions suggest immunosuppression.

questions.q: A 32-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis with non-tender rubbery inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy is positive. Serology: VDRL reactive 1:16, TPHA positive. Stage and treatment?
opts: Secondary syphilis; doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days
Primary syphilis; Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
Lymphogranuloma venereum; doxycycline 100 mg BD × 21 days
questions.exp: The classic painless indurated chancre with non-tender lymphadenopathy and positive dark-field microscopy/serology = primary syphilis. Treatment: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose (WHO/NACO guideline).

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with painful genital ulcer with ragged undermined edges and tender fluctuant inguinal lymph nodes (buboes). Gram stain of bubo aspirate shows 'school of fish' pattern. Diagnosis and treatment?
opts: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi); azithromycin 1g single dose or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM
questions.exp: Chancroid caused by H. ducreyi presents with painful soft ulcer and tender buboes. Gram stain shows gram-negative rods in 'school of fish/railway track' arrangement. Treatment: azithromycin 1g PO single dose or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM.

questions.q: A 26-year-old man from south India presents with painless beefy-red ulcer on the genitalia with rolled everted edges and no lymphadenopathy. Tissue smear shows bipolar staining 'safety-pin' bodies within mononuclear cells. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Donovanosis (Granuloma inguinale) caused by Klebsiella granulomatis shows Donovan bodies (intracytoplasmic, bipolar safety-pin staining) in mononuclear cells on Giemsa-stained tissue crush smear. No lymphadenopathy (pseudobuboes are subcutaneous granulomas). Treatment: azithromycin or doxycycline × ≥3 weeks.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with a malar rash, oral ulcers, and photosensitivity. ANA titre is 1:320 with anti-dsDNA positivity. DIF of lesional skin shows granular IgG, IgM, and C3 at the DEJ. This DIF finding is termed:
questions.exp: The 'lupus band test' refers to granular immune deposits (IgG, IgM, C3) at the DEJ seen on DIF. Positive in lesional skin in SLE and also in non-lesional sun-exposed skin in systemic LE (helps distinguish SLE from DLE).

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules over knuckles, and shawl sign. Which investigation is the most specific marker for this condition?
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis-specific antibodies include anti-Mi-2 (classic DM, photodistributed rash), anti-Jo-1 (antisynthetase syndrome, ILD), anti-MDA5 (amyopathic DM, severe ILD). Anti-Mi-2 is highly specific for classic dermatomyositis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, thickening of skin of fingers (sclerodactyly), telangiectasias, and dysphagia. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. This corresponds to which CREST component?
questions.exp: CREST = Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia — a form of limited cutaneous SSc. Anti-centromere antibody is characteristic (70-80%). Pulmonary hypertension is the main complication, unlike diffuse SSc which has renal crisis/ILD.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectases on the nose. The centre has ulcerated with a 'rodent' appearance. Histology shows peripheral palisading of tumour cells. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer. The noduloulcerative ('rodent ulcer') type shows pearlescent border with telangiectases, central ulceration, and peripheral nuclear palisading on histology. Sun-exposed skin of head and neck is the classic location.

questions.q: A 68-year-old immunosuppressed renal transplant recipient develops a rapidly growing keratinising ulcerating lesion on the back of the hand. Histology shows invasive squamous cell nests with keratin pearls. The main risk factor specific to this patient?
questions.exp: Organ transplant recipients have a 65-250× increased risk of SCC due to chronic immunosuppression (especially calcineurin inhibitors like cyclosporine, tacrolimus) and HPV synergy. SCC in transplant recipients is more aggressive and metastasises earlier.

questions.q: A 45-year-old presents with an asymmetric pigmented lesion: ABCDs present, diameter 8 mm, evolving over 3 months. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, regression structures, and blue-white veil. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is indicated when Breslow thickness exceeds:
questions.exp: Per AJCC 8th edition, SLNB is recommended for melanomas ≥0.8 mm Breslow thickness (or <0.8 mm with ulceration or high mitotic rate). SLNB is the most important prognostic procedure for clinically node-negative patients.

questions.q: A 62-year-old male presents with generalised erythroderma, intense pruritus, and palpable lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood flow cytometry shows CD4+/CD7- cells >1000/μL with Sézary cells on smear. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Sézary syndrome is the leukaemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL). Defined by triad: erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and circulating Sézary cells (CD4+/CD26-/CD7- cells ≥1000/μL). EBV negative; HTLV-1 negative (distinguishes from ATLL).

questions.q: During a patch test for allergic contact dermatitis, which reading time is considered the most important for accurate interpretation?
questions.exp: ICDRG recommends readings at D2 (48h) and D3-D4 (72-96h). The D3/D4 reading is considered most important as it captures late reactions and distinguishes irritant (fades by D4) from allergic reactions (persist or intensify). Late readings at D7 are needed for metals (neomycin, gold).

questions.q: A dermatologist uses Wood's lamp (365 nm UV-A) to examine a patient. Which of the following conditions shows coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp?
questions.exp: Erythrasma caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum fluoresces coral-red under Wood's lamp due to coproporphyrin III production. Pityriasis versicolor: golden-yellow. M. canis tinea capitis: blue-green. Pseudomonas: green fluorescence.

questions.q: During Mohs micrographic surgery, what is the unique advantage that makes it the treatment of choice for morphoeic basal cell carcinoma?
opts: It provides the highest cosmetic outcome by using laser energy
It allows 100% margin examination with real-time histological mapping
It delivers targeted radiotherapy to tumour margins
It uses cryotherapy to destroy tumour edges
questions.exp: Mohs surgery examines 100% of peripheral and deep surgical margins using horizontal frozen sections and tissue mapping. This allows immediate re-excision of positive margins with maximum tissue conservation. Cure rate >99% for primary BCC vs ~90% for standard excision.

questions.q: A patient on long-term dapsone develops pallor and fatigue. G6PD assay shows severe deficiency. Which haematological complication is most directly linked to this combination?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent methaemoglobinaemia and haemolysis in ALL patients, but G6PD deficiency dramatically worsens haemolytic anaemia because G6PD is needed to replenish NADPH for RBC protection against oxidative stress. Baseline G6PD testing before dapsone initiation is mandatory.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman with moderate-severe acne is prescribed isotretinoin. The most critical mandatory precaution before initiating therapy is:
opts: Two forms of contraception and negative pregnancy test (iPLEDGE protocol)
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a category X teratogen. The iPLEDGE/pregnancy prevention programme mandates two effective contraceptive methods, negative urine/serum β-hCG within 30 days before therapy, and monthly during treatment. LFT and lipids are also monitored but pregnancy prevention is the most critical step.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis involving 30% BSA fails methotrexate. She is started on adalimumab. Which pre-biologic screening investigation is MANDATORY in India?
opts: Chest X-ray and tuberculin skin test (TST)/IGRA for latent TB
questions.exp: All TNF-alpha inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept) can reactivate latent TB. Screening with CXR and TST/IGRA is mandatory before initiating biologics in India (high TB burden country). Latent TB must be treated for ≥4 weeks before starting the biologic.

questions.q: A 28-year-old presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery micaceous scales on the extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees. Auspitz sign is positive. Which histological finding is pathognomonic of psoriasis?
opts: Parakeratosis, Munro's microabscesses, and suprapapillary thinning
Dyskeratotic cells in the granular layer
questions.exp: Psoriasis histology shows: regular acanthosis, suprapapillary thinning, loss of granular layer, parakeratosis, Munro's microabscesses (PMNs in stratum corneum), and Kogoj's spongiform pustule in spinous layer. The combination is pathognomonic.

questions.q: A 30-year-old presents with recurrent episodes of urticaria and angioedema precipitated by stress and NSAIDs for over 8 weeks. Total serum IgE is normal. Autologous serum skin test is positive. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Urticaria lasting >6 weeks = chronic urticaria. Positive ASST indicates autoimmune CSU with circulating IgG anti-FcεRIα or anti-IgE antibodies (~35-40% of CSU). Normal IgE rules out IgE-mediated atopic disease. Hereditary angioedema lacks wheals and has low C4/C1-INH.

questions.q: A 50-year-old presents with palpable purpura on the lower legs, arthralgias, and haematuria. Skin biopsy shows leucocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposition on DIF. Serum IgA is elevated. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is defined by palpable purpura + ≥1 of: diffuse abdominal pain, arthritis, renal involvement, or IgA-predominant immune deposits on biopsy (EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria). Most common vasculitis in children; renal involvement determines prognosis.
